author: Agencies
description:
• American saves three set points in second-set rally

  • Gauff wins six straight games to seal 6-4, 7-5 victory

  • World No 4 needs Noskova help to reach last four

Coco Gauff clawed out a 6-4, 7-5 round-robin victory over Marta Kostyuk on Thursday to keep her WTA Finals hopes alive in Indian Wells, California.

The world No 4 still needs help to reach the semi-finals of the elite season-ending event. If fifth-ranked compatriot Jessica Pegula beats Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in Thursday’s final group match, Pegula will advance instead. Noskova has already qualified.

Continue reading...
title: Gauff saves three set points to beat Kostyuk and keep WTA Finals hopes alive

author: Rachel Aroesti
description:
This sensationally idiotic guide to film history is hilarious. From a crude Mary Poppins gag to confusing the hell out of Michael Bay, I could listen to Cunk’s surreal tosh all day

In a world of slow-burn, jargon-littered dramas, there’s something to be said for the TV programme that sets out its stall within the first 12 seconds. Cunk on Cinema is one such programme. The latest series from Diane Morgan’s sensationally idiotic documentarian is a three-part history of film that begins with our host reeling off some of humanity’s greatest achievements in her deadpan Bolton tones. Specifically, “conquering the landscape, growing the great wall of Chinese, discovering Mona Lisa and inventing global warming”. If you think that list is funny, you’ll enjoy what is essentially a vehicle for some of the stupidest jokes ever written. If you find that kind of malapropism and misapprehension childish, I suggest you switch off immediately.

We first encountered Philomena Cunk in 201
title: Cunk on Cinema review – Diane Morgan baffles Hollywood with some of the stupidest jokes ever told

author: Sarah Dempster
description:
For a drama that is meant to explore female trauma, Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are given very little to do as small-town lawyers. It is Gleeson who steals the show as their broken father who earns the name Shatticus Finch

“Why is ma laaahf filled with contrary feee-males?” grumbles dilapidated defence lawyer Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson), his deep south vowels stretching like grilled cheese across his cluttered desk.

Poor Rusty. As the father of two headstrong lawyer daughters, this sunken beanbag of fading masculinity is forced daily to endure the contrariness of feee-males who are forever challengin’ the status quo. “This is all bullshit,” snaps elder daughter Sam (Rose Byrne), by way of illustration. “You’re a dipshit,” adds Charlie (Meghann Fahy), thoughtfully. They sure don’t make his laaahf easy! But the sisters love ol’ Rusty, or at least do their best to tolerate his excruciating aphorisms (“Never kick
title: The Good Daughter review – the best thing about this legal thriller? Brendan Gleeson’s sad toilet fart

author: Suzanne Wrack at the Camp Nou
description:
Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, digging deep to hold on to a draw here. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared.

The last time these two teams met, Arsenal were lifting aloft the Champions League trophy at Barcelona’s expense after the most perfect of defensive performances and a Stina Blackstenius goal in Lisbon in 2025. It was a far less perfect defensive performance this time, but Arsenal showed guts against the team that retook their crown last season and showed they can play ugly when needed.

Continue reading...
title: Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance

author: Presented by Lucy Hough with George Chidi ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. How did Colom’s grassroots campaign win despite limited early backing from national Democrats? Lucy Hough speaks to politics and democracy reporter George Chidi

Continue reading...
title: Mississippi makes history with Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win - The Latest

author: Dan Collyns in Chiclayo
description:
Pope Leo XIV is visiting the country, where he spent nearly a decade as bishop, during an 11-day South American tour

The walls in Chiclayo have been painted with colourful murals and banners welcoming Pope Leo XIV, but he is better known to residents of this city in northern Peru as “Padre Roberto” – a pastor who walked their streets, shared their love of local cuisine, and stood by them through natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Robert Prevost, 71, who spent nearly a decade as the bishop here until he left in 2023, now returns as the Catholic church’s most powerful figure. Yet for the city’s faithful he remains humble and approachable, the characteristics that first endeared him to them.

Continue reading...
title: Pope Leo gets rapturous welcome in Peru: ‘This visit is like a big party’

author: Editorial
description:
The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied

What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals, which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared.

The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence.
title: The Guardian view on Gaza’s misery: don’t let Palestinian deaths mount in this bleak winter | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs

Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry.

The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a
title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial

author: John Crace
description:
It’s not been a good week for Farage. Aside from that interview and disrespect from the BBC, he’s lost another senior Reform official

It’s a day late, but please observe a two-minute silence for Nigel Farage. Lest we forget. Sad to say, but Nige just hasn’t been quite the same since Sunday’s Remembrance service at the Cenotaph. Like me, you might have thought that he had been in Whitehall to honour those who had died in two world wars and subsequent armed conflicts. Only it turns out he was really there to commemorate himself.

Through his personal valet, Richard Tice, Nige has let it be known that he was extremely angry with the BBC’s coverage of the service. The cameras had spent too long lingering on the faces of the king, other members of the royal family and prime ministers past and present. When what they should have been focused on throughout was Nige. He was the one we were all there to see. The man who had done more for his country than anyone else. To
title: Spare a thought for poor Nige, clearly missing his podcast chats with Russell Brand

author: Nils Pratley
description:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

Continue reading...
title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley

author: Anthony Hayward
description:
Burly TV presenter who brought his building knowledge and power tools to the BBC’s gardening makeover show Ground Force

Tommy Walsh, who has died aged 69, brought decking and pergolas, as well as rippling muscles and a brusque manner, to the BBC gardening show Ground Force, alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock. The trio transformed gardens for members of the public in just two days, and the programme (which ran from 1997 until 2005) made the burly 6ft 5in Walsh a star after years running his own building and landscaping business. “People want textures, shapes and surfaces in the garden that you wouldn’t get from planting alone,” he said.

Armed with a power drill, sledgehammer and a host of other tools, he did the back-breaking landscaping work before Titchmarsh, the gardener and broadcaster, and Charlie Dimmock, a garden centre worker, moved in to do the planting. Homeowners would go away and return to find the results of the surprise makeover, organised clande
title: Tommy Walsh obituary

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Only three retained in same positions from Australia game

  • ‘We want the very best of these guys,’ says Maro Itoje

England’s World Cup hopefuls have been warned not to go off script when auditioning for a place on the plane next year after Steve Borthwick rang the changes to his side to face Japan on Saturday, handing starts to rookies Will Joseph and Max Ojomoh as well as Henry Pollock.

Borthwick has made 10 personnel and two positional changes to his team to play Eddie Jones’s side with a glut of injuries, a handful of players in need of a rest and the head coach’s determination to give those such as Joseph and Ojomoh, who line up on the right wing and inside centre respectively, the chance to shine. Pollock makes his second start, coming in at No 8, while the Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland is in line for a debut from the bench.
title: Much-changed England told to ignore World Cup and put team first against Japan

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to Simon Jenkins’s article suggesting that parliament should relocate out of London

Simon Jenkins is right to characterise parliament as “outdated and immune to reform” (Notre-Dame was restored in five years and under budget. But the Palace of Westminster? No chance, 6 November). However, it is not only cost, practicality and design that are compelling reasons to empty the building and move to purpose-built premises. The building and the institution in their present form are entirely inappropriate for the workplace of a modern democracy.

The self-entitlement evident in the resistance to moving out, such as that voiced by, among others, Jacob Rees-Mogg, illustrates the assumptions of class and leadership roles in those most comfortable with the status quo, and with the arcane, outdated building and rituals, which must seem bizarre and
title: Why parliament needs to move out – and move on | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by Fiona Harvey in which she questioned whether progress is being made 10 years on from the Paris treaty

As world leaders gathered in Turkey for the UN climate talks, Fiona Harvey was right to ask, “What’s the point?” (What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?, 7 November). She pointed to how over 10 years ago in Paris, countries came together for the 21st conference and signed an agreement that aimed to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. For the past two years, temperatures “have exceeded that threshold”.

I was at last year’s climate summit in Brazil, where it was obvious that the Cop process itself is a big part of the problem. The agreed text did not
title: We need to rethink climate action away from the Cop talks | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Clem Cattini, who played on more than 40 No 1 hits as a session musician, was very modest about his talent, writes Mark Sweet. Plus a letter from DLL Gould

Working as a propman on Blue Peter in 1998, I was privileged to witness a performance of Remember You’re a Womble by the furry pop band as they prepared for a nationwide tour.

During a break in rehearsals I chatted to a heavily sweating Bungo on the drum kit. “By the way,” I asked him, “what do you do when you’re not being a Womble?”

Continue reading...
title: Clem Cattini: remember he was a Womble – and almost a member of Led Zeppelin | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
William Rees says Ealing council’s workshops have shown that even an hour spent on a creative pursuit can change someone’s day

Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Continue reading...
title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter

author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
description:
Andy Burnham’s newly appointed climate adviser used report to warn of national security risk from collapsing ecosystems

The UK government still has no plans to publish an explosive report showing the national security risk from the collapse of ecosystems around the world – even after handing the key official behind the report a new advisory role.

Andy Burnham addressed the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Thursday and said the UK was determined to reach net zero by 2050 and work with its partners to build a clean energy future.

Continue reading...
title: UK ministers have no plans to publish explosive report on climate crisis

author: Andy Bull
description:
Injury crisis makes the job harder for Fabien Galthié whose side have beaten South Africa once in their last 10 meetings

The final of this inaugural Nations Championship is two weeks away, but regardless of who makes it through to the last match at Twickenham there’s an irresistible sense that the two best teams from either side of the competition will go head-to-head at the Stade de France this Friday night. France, back-to-back Six Nations champions, play South Africa, back-to-back world champions, and the one team that the French – and anyone else with dreams of becoming the world’s best team – need to find a way to beat in the 12 months before the Springboks take a run at winning a third consecutive World Cup.

France have been looking for one of those for a long time now. This is not an even-sided rivalry. South Africa have won nine of the 10 games the two teams have played in the last 15 years, including the last five in Paris. England, Ireland, even Wales all have
title: France have spent years trying to beat the Boks but belief and bodies are fading

author: Presented by Kiran Stacey and Jessica Elgot, produced by Saskia Collette, music by Axel Kacoutié; executive producer Maz Ebtehaj
description:
This week, Kemi Badenoch roasted the prime minister at PMQs with gag after gag. But while the leader of the opposition looks feisty, are some Labour MPs also beginning to wonder if Andy Burnham has the substance to back his policy agenda?

Plus, with the social media ban looking likely to include companies such as Vinted, deputy political editor Jessica Elgot explains the government’s thinking

Read Kiran’s article on jitters about Burnham’s 10-year plan here

Read Jessica’s article on the social media ban here

Send any questions for Pippa and Kiran to politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com

Watch Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel
title: Are cracks showing in the Burnham project? – podcast

author: John Ashdown
description:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Tuesday 22 April 2014: “Manchester United has announced that David Moyes has left the club. The club would like to place on record its thanks for the hard work, honesty and integrity he brought to the role.”

Oh no! Where will the USA! USA! USA! ever be able to find a manager who could lead us to the dizzying heights of yet another humiliating defeat in the round of 16? A completely empty safari shirt on a clothes hanger could do that. Now he’s leaving the national team to prioritise a club team, which is exactly what he criticised Christian Pulisic for doing a while back. A $10m dollar buyout from Manchester United is a way more appealing prospect than another World Cup cycle with this guy. Adios, Mauricio. I’d add gracias, but for what, exactly?” – Chi.

If any Manchester United fans
title: Football Daily | ‘The club would like to thank …’: Manchester United dust off the heartfelt exit message

author: Polly Toynbee
description:
‘I look out for my team,’ a store manager tells me, but Poundland’s US owner doesn’t care. Labour may be too late to prevent it becoming yet another casualty of venture capital

In the Poundland I visit, a treasure trove of bargains, the staff are dejected. The shelves are emptying because the owners have withheld £50m needed for new stock and paying wages. It’s just one of 600 stores in peril, and these employees just a few of 12,000 at risk of losing their jobs – with 30,000 jobs at risk in supply chains.

On Tuesday £10m was released: not enough, but preventing instant collapse. Gordon Brothers, the US owner that bought Poundland for a symbolic £1 last year, specialises in buying and “rest
title: Look at the Poundland scandal and see a crisis that goes beyond Britain’s high streets | Polly Toynbee

author: Sali Hughes
description:
Whether its bargain stocking fillers or a lipstick worth splashing out on, our beauty editor reveals what she’d love to give – and receive

• The best Christmas gifts for mums, grannies, aunties and friends

Bella Freud x Boots hand duo, 2 x 345ml

Continue reading...
title: From cult skincare to seriously posh soap: Sali Hughes’s best beauty gifts for Christmas 2026

author: Fiona Sturges
description:
Actor Seth Numrich vividly captures the neurotic tendencies of a middle-aged man with a digital dependency, in an intense multilayered tale of family and storytelling

We meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t be interviewed again. The narrator confesses to his young daughter, Eva, that he is nervous about the meeting. Those nerves are replaced by panic when he gets to his hotel and drops his iPhone into a sink of water, rendering it useless. Not only does he have no means of recording the interview, he won’t be able to FaceTime Eva at bedtime.

Ben Lerner’s novella is a thoughtful meditation on memory, storytelling and lives lived through technology. The middle-aged narrator’s anxiety over his phone falls away as he engages with the world around him and with his past. He is pleased
title: Transcription by Ben Lerner audiobook review – a mediation on memory for the smartphone era

author: Phil Hoad
description:
Ahead of the UK release of Nathan Fielder’s hotly anticipated Elizabeth Holmes flick, we count down the most shocking and affecting true stories ever committed to film

A 50-second dispatch from daily life blew the whistle on the approaching juggernaut of cinema and its unbeatable horsepower of verisimilitude. But if we must be strictly factual about the iconic Lumière brothers’ short, the anecdote about audience members fleeing their seats in fear of being crushed by the oncoming locomotive probably never happened.

Continue reading...
title: You can see everything on this list: the 20 most jaw-dropping documentaries – ranked!

author: Mina Holland
description:
Five wines that hit the spot without breaking the bank

Last week, I made The One Sauce from the new Ottolenghi book, Simple Too, and it might well be the zenith of tomato sauces. We ate this gloriously garlicky, vinegar-spiked number with pasta, and it was a revelation. After one bite, it felt rude not to have some wine with it and, before I knew it, I had a glass of red in front of me.

Today, I am championing school-night wine. Not because I want to be a bad influence, but because, in this restrained, over-scheduled, all-or-nothing age, we risk losing the impromptu pleasure of a nice drop – with food, say, or with a friend who has popped by, or just to offset the nervous strain of the children’s bedtime. Occasionally, “It’s a school night” is reason enough to do something.
title: School-night wine - the best bottles for an impromptu midweek treat

author: Flora Willson
description:
Coventry Cathedral
Kazuki Yamada led the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra and chorus and soloists Christian Gerhaher, Andrew Staples and Olga Peretyatko in this monumental and moving performance of Britten’s towering work

The premiere of Britten’s War Requiem as part of the consecration of Coventry’s new cathedral in 1962 left its German baritone soloist Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau “completely undone”. Sculptor Barbara Hepworth listened on the radio and declared herself “profoundly moved”. The composer described it as a “call for peace”; critics unanimously
title: War Requiem review – in the cathedral where it premiered, Britten’s masterpiece has lost none of its power

author: Ed Aarons
description:
• Thomas Frank the leading contender to take over

  • Palace have conceded league-high 24 goals

Pierre Sage has been sacked as Crystal Palace’s manager after 16 games. The Frenchman, appointed in mid-June to replace Oliver Glasner, has gone after Sunday’s 3-1 defeat by Liverpool left his team bottom of the Premier League.

Thomas Frank, out of work since his dismissal by Spurs in February, has emerged as the main candidate to succeed Sage. He spoke to Palace in the summer and is said to be keen for a new challenge after a successful spell at Brentford.

Continue reading...
title: Pierre Sage sacked by Crystal Palace after 16 games with club bottom of league

author: Aaron Bower
description:
England go into Friday’s final against France hopeful of retaining their title – and inspiring more to take up their fast-growing, compelling sport

Sport in Britain is so often judged on various key metrics. Attendances, TV viewing figures, revenue and, arguably the most important one of all, trophies. On Friday morning, a group of men will represent England in a World Cup final, hoping to retain the trophy they won in 2022 while still playing for something far more important.

The captain of England’s rugby league wheelchair team, Lewis King, remembers what things used to be like as a wheelchair athlete. His life changed in 2009 when, aged 24, he was left partially paralysed after a blood clot on his spine that required an emergency operation. At that stage, playing sport felt impossible, let alone leading England in a World Cup final against France in Australia.
title: World Cup triumph would only be half the story for England’s wheelchair rugby league squad

author: Adrian Chiles
description:
Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others?

How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation.

The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and
title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles

author: Presented by Ian Sample with Madeleine Finlay , produced by Joshan Chana, Luke John Smith and Jacob Liebenberg , graphics by Elliot Ellis, the executive producer was Ellie Bury
description:
As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting in Turkey for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. Madeleine Finlay tells co-host Ian Sample why these negotiations are so critical and what the chances are of meaningful change.

Continue reading...
title: Cop31: how far off target are we? - video

author: Press Association
description:
• Veteran bowler was released by Lancashire

  • ‘I can’t wait to start a new chapter in my career’

Jimmy Anderson will continue his career in 2027 after signing to play for Surrey.

England men’s all-time leading wicket taker was released by Lancashire at the end of the 2026 season. But the 44-year-old will play on after agreeing a deal at the Kia Oval.

More to follow

Continue reading...
title: ‘I have a lot to offer’: 44-year-old Jimmy Anderson joins Surrey for 2027

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
The latest film version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol is decent enough, though its star is rather better as the legendary miser before redemption arrives

Here for lovers of Dickens – and fans of subtext – is an unexpectedly watchable new movie version of A Christmas Carol starring a top-hatted and heavily madeup Johnny Depp; it is a film about whether it’s possible for a man to earn redemption before it is too late. (The answer is … sure, as long as you say sorry and change your ways. But Mr Scrooge never launched a libel action against the Sun for calling him an un-Christmassy old meanie.)

In fact, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern and director Ti West have put together a perfectly serviceable, faithful adaptation – a tradaptation, if you will – of Dickens’s masterpiece about the hideous old miser saved from damnation on Ch
title: Ebenezer review – Johnny Depp’s Scrooge tries to exorcise ghosts of business past

author: Jesse Hassenger
description:
The US midterms made it into this week’s episode, which focuses on gay couple Craig and Tweek as they join a ‘pay-to-play’ sport team which promises them a better future

South Park (or South America, as it’s known this season) is renowned for its turning around episodes far quicker than just about any scripted series, resulting in some of the most topical humor attempted on TV this side of Saturday Night Live. The “blue wave” in the US midterms one week ago made it into the start of this week’s episode – but they are not discussed much more than that, because Donald Trump suffered a big defeat and “it’s no fun punching down on a helpless loser”.

But it does mean the return of PC Principal, who delivers a funny torrent of profanities and belligerent vows of diversity and tolerance in a hyper-emboldened liberal version of the right-wing gloating we’ve seen in past elect
title: South Park takes on the expensive, confusing world of club sports – with a nod to Heated Rivalry

author: Phil Harrison, Priya Elan and Ali Catterall
description:
More hilarious misinformation from Diane Morgan’s comedy creation. Plus: the beefy history between rockstar chefs. Here’s what to watch this evening

10pm, BBC Two
Diane Morgan’s stealthy ascent to national treasure status has been supercharged by her brilliant comedy Ann Droid. And now she returns to the faux-bewildered world of Philomena Cunk. “For centuries, eyes were useless,” Cunk states. “Because there was nothing worth looking at.” So begins a film history lesson that incorporates comic misinformation and contributions from the likes of Mark Cousins and Benedict Cumberbatch – who are surely in on the joke? Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: Philomena Cunk is back – and taking on Hollywood

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
Four free exhibitions take you from a luxury white enclave in Rio de Janeiro to exhausted erotic dancers touring the US and a culture-changing London address

★★★★☆

Continue reading...
title: ‘You can almost smell the sweat’: striptease artists and steel pans light up this week’s free art shows

author: Sara Hudston
description:
Exmoor, Somerset: Tarr Steps is no stranger to flooding, but the damage is becoming more and more frequent

Fog cloaked the combe as we walked down to the River Barle, and for the first time in months I wished I were wearing gloves. A red kite wheeled overhead, the dull copper colour of its underparts matching the autumn leaves still clinging to the oaks. Red kites are still fairly uncommon on Exmoor, though their numbers have increased recently as the species pushes west. Several pheasants whirred past, calling loudly in alarm: they are also more numerous now, due to the spread of game-shooting estates.

We were heading for Tarr Steps, the longest clapper bridge in Britain, an ancient footbridge nearly 55 metres long, with 17 arches braced across the Barle. It is constructed of pillars of piled rock set about two metres apart, spanned by huge, flat gritstones weighing up to two tonnes each. The whole edifice is held together by bulk and weight, with
title: Country diary: An ancient bridge, laid low by one storm after another | Sara Hudston

author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Dan Milmo; produced by Ruth Abrahams, Tom Glasser and Brian McNamara; executive producer Sami Kent
description:
Global technology editor Dan Milmo on the scandal rocking the world of AI: US intelligence believes the lover of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, is a Chinese spy

Nvidia is one of the biggest companies in the world. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, is worth around $150bn (£112bn). But the AI giant’s stock is sliding – and Huang’s position is under question – after it emerged on Sunday that he had been having an affair with a woman US intelligence services believe is a Chinese spy.

Global technology editor Dan Milmo talks through the scandal that has rocked both Silicon Valley and the financial markets.

Continue reading...
title: The (alleged) spy who loved me: the Nvidia scandal - podcast
